title: Prefix sums
sub: Subarray Sum Equals K and Product of Array Except Self: a prefix in a dictionary, a prefix and a suffix without division
cards/0/title: Subarray Sum Equals K: the problem and its signals
cards/0/body:
Subarray Sum Equals K (LeetCode #560). Given an integer array nums and a number k, how many contiguous subarrays sum to exactly k? n ≤ 2·10⁴, elements from −1000 to 1000 — negatives occur. Example: [1, 1, 1], k = 2 → 2.

Signals: “contiguous subarray” and “sum” mean sums of segments, and those are conveniently obtained as a difference of prefix sums. “How many” means a counter.

Why not a window. A sliding window works in O(n) by moving the right edge while the sum is below k and the left edge when it is above. That is only valid if widening the window never decreases the sum, that is, if the numbers are non-negative. With a −7 in the array the sum can drop after widening, and the rule “the sum is too big — shrink” throws away segments that would still reach k.

The naive solution: for every start i, extend the end j and keep a running sum. There are about n²/2 pairs (i, j) — for n = 2·10⁴ that is 2·10⁸ additions, right at the edge of the time limit.
cards/1/q: What breaks the sliding window in this problem?
cards/1/options/0: Negative numbers: after widening, the sum can decrease, and shrinking on “sum above k” loses answers
cards/1/options/1: Speed: the window runs in O(n²), and O(n) is required
cards/1/options/2: A window can find only one subarray, it cannot count them all
cards/1/explain: A window relies on monotonicity: wider means a bigger sum, narrower a smaller one. Then once the sum exceeds k, widening further is pointless and the left edge can move. A negative number breaks that monotonicity: [5, −3, 1] with k = 3 gives a sum of 5, above 3, already at the first element; the window drops the 5 — and loses [5, −3, 1] = 3.
cards/1/wrong/1: A window is O(n): each edge crosses the array once. The problem is correctness, not speed.
cards/1/wrong/2: A window can count — with positive numbers it would cope. It is the sign of the numbers that breaks it.
cards/2/title: A prefix in a dictionary: Two Sum on sums
cards/2/body:
Let sum be the sum of the elements from the start up to and including the current j — the prefix sum. The sum of the segment nums[i..j] is the prefix up to j minus the prefix up to i − 1. So a segment ending at j sums to k exactly when a prefix equal to sum − k has occurred before.

This is Two Sum from the first lesson, only on prefixes: for the current sum look up the partner sum − k by exact value. The one difference is that we need not an index but how many times that prefix occurred: each occurrence is a separate segment start. A “prefix → how many times” dictionary. The counter is incremented like this: seen[sum] = seen.GetValueOrDefault(sum) + 1 — GetValueOrDefault returns 0 for a new key (available since .NET Core 2.0 and in .NET Standard 2.1, so in Unity too).

The empty prefix. Before the first element the sum is 0 — it has already “occurred” once, so the dictionary starts as {0: 1}. Without it, segments starting at index 0 are lost.

Invariant: before step j the dictionary holds every prefix ending left of j, plus the empty one. So, as in Two Sum, check first, then insert. Time O(n), memory O(n). Negative numbers no longer matter: the dictionary does not care whether the sum rises or falls. No overflow: |sum| ≤ 2·10⁴ · 1000 = 2·10⁷; with larger values keep prefixes in long.

In a game: prefix sums are the path length to every waypoint (the point “at distance d along the path” is found through the prefixes) and the cumulative weights of a loot table.
cards/3/explain: The {0: 1} start is the empty prefix, the start for segments beginning at index 0. The partner of the current prefix is sum − k. We add times, not 1: every earlier occurrence of the prefix is a separate segment. And we increment the current prefix’s counter rather than write 1: otherwise repeated prefixes (plentiful with negative numbers) would lose their past occurrences.
cards/4/task: Step through the trace on [3, 4, −7, 1, 3, 3, 1, −4], k = 7. The rig stops twice and asks what the code does next: answer from the prefix dictionary on screen.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: count += 1: prefix 0 is already in the dictionary
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: count stays, seen[0] stays 1: the key already exists
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: x = −7: sum becomes 0, need = 0 − 7 = −7. What does the code do?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: We look up need = −7, and no such prefix occurred — count does not grow. But prefix 0 has occurred before (the empty one) and now occurs a second time: its counter becomes 2. That is the difference from Two Sum: we do not overwrite, we count — both zeros will later serve as segment starts.
cards/4/goal/asks/1/q: x = 3: sum = 7, need = 7 − 7 = 0. By how much does count grow?
cards/4/goal/asks/1/explain: Prefix 0 occurred twice: the empty one (before index 0) and the one after −7 (index 2). Each is its own segment start: [3, 4, −7, 1, 3, 3] and [1, 3, 3], both summing to 7. count = 1 + 2 = 3.
cards/5/q: On nums = [1, 2], k = 0 this code returns 2, although no subarray sums to 0. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/5/explain: The prefix goes in before the check, which breaks the invariant “the map holds only what is left of j”. With k = 0 we look up sum − 0 = sum — and find the prefix just stored: an empty segment. With k ≠ 0 the order happens not to matter (sum − k ≠ sum), so the bug survives until the first test with k = 0. The same trap as target = 2x in Two Sum: TryGetValue first, then seen[sum].
cards/6/title: Product of Array Except Self: a prefix and a suffix
cards/6/body:
Product of Array Except Self (LeetCode #238). Return an array ans where ans[i] is the product of all elements except nums[i], in O(n) and without division. n ≤ 10⁵, elements from −30 to 30, and the product of any prefix and suffix is guaranteed to fit in an int. Follow-up: O(1) extra memory, the output array does not count.

Why not division. “Multiply everything and divide by nums[i]” is forbidden by the statement, and for good reason: one zero, and at its position we divide 0 by 0 (DivideByZeroException), while the right answer there is the product of the rest. Zeros can be handled separately, but that is three code branches instead of one idea.

Idea: ans[i] = (product of everything left of i) × (product of everything right of i). The first pass, left to right, carries prefix and writes it into ans. The second pass, right to left, carries suffix and multiplies it in. Invariant: before step i, prefix is the product strictly left of i and suffix strictly right of it. So in both passes we write into ans[i] first and multiply by nums[i] afterwards — otherwise the element ends up in its own product.

Time O(n), extra memory O(1): two variables besides the answer. The same “prefix + suffix” trick shows up in Trapping Rain Water (the two pointers unit), only with a maximum instead of a product.
cards/7/q: Assemble Product of Array Except Self: two passes, no division.
cards/7/explain: There is nothing left of element zero — the empty product is 1, not 0. ans[i] gets prefix as it is: it does not contain nums[i] yet, while prefix * nums[i] would include the element itself. The backward pass starts at the last index n − 1 (starting at n is out of bounds). And suffix is multiplied by nums[i] only after the write — for the next step to the left.
cards/8/task: Step through the trace on [2, 3, 0, 4] — with the zero that breaks division. The rig stops twice and asks what the code does next: answer from prefix and suffix on screen.
cards/8/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: ans[2] = 6, and prefix stays 6: the zero is skipped
cards/8/goal/asks/0/q: i = 2, nums[2] = 0, prefix = 6. What does the code do?
cards/8/goal/asks/0/explain: Write first, multiply after: ans[2] gets the product strictly to the left — 2 · 3 = 6, the zero is not in it. Then prefix × 0 = 0, and everything to the right gets a zero from the left — as it should: for them the zero is among “the rest”.
cards/8/goal/asks/1/q: Backward pass, i = 2: ans[2] = 6, suffix = 4. What is written into ans[2]?
cards/8/goal/asks/1/explain: suffix is the product strictly right of i, that is, just 4: the zero joins suffix on the next line. ans[2] = 6 · 4 = 24 — the product of everything but the zero. The rest get 0: for i = 3 the zero sits in prefix, for i = 1 and i = 0 in suffix. Answer [0, 0, 24, 0].
cards/9/body:
Many range sum queries (Range Sum Query, #303): build an array of prefixes P of length n + 1 once, with P[0] = 0; after that the sum of [l..r] = P[r + 1] − P[l] in O(1).

The longest subarray summing to k (#325): a “prefix → first index” dictionary. The segment length is j minus the index of prefix sum − k, and the further left that index, the longer the segment. So the index is written on the prefix’s first occurrence and never overwritten. Contiguous Array (#525) belongs here too: the longest segment with equal numbers of 0s and 1s — replace 0 with −1, and the problem becomes “the longest subarray summing to 0”.

A sum divisible by k (#974): a segment is divisible by k when two prefixes have the same remainder. The key is the remainder, the start is remainder 0 once. A C# trap: % keeps the sign of the dividend, -7 % 5 == -2, so normalize: ((sum % k) + k) % k. There are only k remainders — an int[k] array is enough instead of a dictionary.

A sum over a rectangle (#304): two-dimensional prefixes. S[y, x] is the sum of all cells above and to the left; a rectangle is assembled from four corners (inclusion–exclusion) in O(1). In a game: “how many walls or units are in this area of the tile map”, “is a 5×5 plot free for a building” — O(1) per query after O(w·h) preparation.
cards/10/q: You solve Subarray Sum Equals K out loud in an interview. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/10/items/0: Clarify: can numbers be negative, what are n, k and the values, does an empty subarray count
cards/10/items/1: Name the brute force over starts and ends with a running sum: O(n²), about 2·10⁸ additions for n = 2·10⁴
cards/10/items/2: Explain why not a window: negative numbers break the monotonicity of the sum
cards/10/items/3: Idea: the segment ending at j sums to k if prefix sum − k occurred before; a “prefix → how many times” dictionary starting at {0: 1}
cards/10/items/4: Write the code: first add seen[sum − k], then increment seen[sum]
cards/10/items/5: Run [1, 1, 1] with k = 2 and state the complexity: O(n) time and memory
cards/10/items/6: Edge cases: k = 0, a segment starting at index 0, sum overflow
cards/10/explain: The statement, the baseline, why the obvious optimization (a window) fails, the idea, the code, an example and the complexity, edge cases. Interviewers expect the window point: it shows you know where a technique stops applying.
cards/11/title: A counter in a dictionary: one lookup instead of two
cards/11/body:
seen[sum] = seen.GetValueOrDefault(sum) + 1 is two lookups by key: a read and a write. Together with TryGetValue for sum − k, that is three hash computations per element. In .NET 6+ the increment takes a single lookup: CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrAddDefault finds the entry or creates it with the default value and returns a ref to the value right inside the dictionary.

Capacity. There are at most n + 1 distinct prefixes — set the capacity up front, and the dictionary will not grow along the way.

Unity (.NET Standard 2.1) has no CollectionsMarshal — there you keep GetValueOrDefault and the indexer, or an array instead of a dictionary if the keys fall in a narrow range.
cards/11/deep:
Why a ref into a dictionary is dangerous. GetValueRefOrAddDefault returns a reference straight into the entries array. While it is alive you must not add or remove keys: on growth the entries move to a new array, while the ref keeps pointing into the old one — the write “gets lost” without any exception. For reading without inserting there is CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrNullRef (also .NET 6+); a missing key is checked with Unsafe.IsNullRef. The same trick in Group Anagrams: ref var list = ref CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrAddDefault(groups, key, out bool exists); if (!exists) list = new List<string>(); — one lookup, and for a string key that means one hashing pass over the string instead of two.

EnsureCapacity and TrimExcess (.NET Core 2.1+, .NET Standard 2.1 — in Unity since 2021.2). EnsureCapacity(n) grows in advance a dictionary that lives in a field and is reused via Clear() — before a batch of inserts, with no re-placing along the way. TrimExcess() gives memory back after a peak: a dictionary that ballooned to 10⁶ entries during level loading keeps the same arrays after Clear() until you shrink it. And Clear() costs O(capacity), not O(number of entries): the whole bucket array is zeroed. A huge dictionary cleared every frame for a dozen entries wastes time.

An array instead of a dictionary. If prefixes fall in a narrow range — in Contiguous Array, for instance, after replacing 0 with −1 the sum lies in [−n, n] — an int[2n + 1] with the index shifted by sum + n replaces the dictionary: no hashes, no collisions, and in Jobs such a counter is a NativeArray<int>, which Burst handles with no restrictions.

Overflow and float. In #560 the sum is at most 2·10⁷ in absolute value — int is enough; in general keep prefixes in long. Prefixes in float — path length, accumulated time — lose precision: the difference of two large, close numbers eats the significant digits. For long routes use double, or measure distances from the nearest reference point rather than from the start.
